title: How Superculture® Pet Oral drives fresher breath in 7 days
summary: We walk through the mechanism behind Superculture® Pet Oral’s breath and oral microbiome benefits.
body_text: Key takeaway Superculture® Pet Oral is the most clinically-validated oral health postbiotic on the market. We designed it to target the root of poor pet oral health: the unwanted microbes in the mouth that generate bad breath and form biofilms. Rather than masking odor or relying on mechanical action, it works directly through the oral microbiome, and it does so fast enough to significantly reduce the compounds behind bad breath in as little as 7 days. Clinical validation in dogs Most oral care products are validated, if at all, on a single endpoint. Superculture® Pet Oral has been tested across five independent double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trials in dogs, spanning the three oral health endpoints that matter most: bad breath and the compounds behind it, oral biofilms, and the oral microbiome itself. The headline results: Fresher breath, fast. The ingredient significantly reduced volatile sulfur compounds (VSCs), the molecules responsible for bad breath, after only 7 days, and by roughly 27% more from baseline than placebo. In the same study, human perception of bad breath tracked with the measured drop in VSCs. It targets unwanted microbes directly. In just 7 days, Superculture® Pet Oral reduced the unwanted microbes that both produce VSCs and generate the biofilms that become plaque and build up into tartar. It promotes a healthy oral microbiome. Across studies, dogs given Superculture® Pet Oral demonstrated: a lower abundance of biofilm-forming and VSC-producing taxa, greater species evenness, and a reduction in Porphyromonas cangingivalis , a microbe closely linked to periodontal disease. In a clean-tooth model over 84 days, Superculture® Pet Oral attenuated an undesirable shift in the oral microbiome by limiting the increase of pathogen-associated taxa by up to 55%. Research from three of our clinical studies has been published in the peer-reviewed journals Animals ( VSC reduction and human perception of bad breath ) and the Journal of Veterinary Dentistry ( Oral microbiome , VSC reduction and human perception of bad breath ). Why we designed around the oral microbiome Nearly 90% of dogs show signs of periodontal disease by age two, and yet most existing pet oral health solutions are ineffective. Fragrant oils temporarily mask odor without impacting what causes it. Mechanical action chips away at plaque at the surface but leaves the underlying root of poor oral health untouched. Broad chemical actives kill microbes indiscriminately, including the beneficial ones a healthy mouth depends on. The insight that shaped our R&D of Superculture® Pet Oral: unwanted microbes in the oral microbiome sit at the root of bad breath and poor oral health. We identified two key mechanisms of action to design an ingredient intentionally targeting poor oral health: (1) suppressing VSC production by the unwanted oral microbes and (2) disrupting oral biofilms that had already formed in the oral cavity. Through extensive screening, we identified a combination of microbes that possessed exceptional functionality through both of these mechanisms of action. Superculture® Pet Oral is the combination of those AAFCO-listed microbial strains, delivered as a postbiotic. It delivers benefits even with brief exposure to the oral cavity, and without mechanical action, making it ideal for the many pets that resist teeth brushing. Confirming performance in canine conditions Before conducting our in vivo clinical studies, we validated Superculture® Pet Oral's mechanisms of action in vitro under canine-relevant oral conditions and within realistic contact times. To ensure a relevant model, we collected oral microbiome samples from dogs, isolated and sequenced individual strains, and selected a native canine strain that is both a strong producer of VSCs and a robust biofilm former to represent the unwanted microbes we set out to target. We then grew established biofilms of that strain and treated them with Superculture® Pet Oral at our recommended, orally-relevant dose. The ingredient delivered on both mechanisms: Biofilm disruption. Superculture® Pet Oral achieved near-complete disruption of oral biofilms, an average reduction of 98%. That performance vastly exceeded eight commonly-used oral health actives tested in parallel, including zinc, brown algae, spirulina, and zeolites, none of which came close. VSC suppression. Superculture® Pet Oral reduced the volatile sulfur compounds behind bad breath by an average of 85%, while common comparators such as spirulina and coenzyme Q10 showed no effect. Relating ingredient design to clinical outcome We hold ourselves to a three-part standard: mechanism-centered design, in vitro screening, and benefit-focused clinical validation on the endpoints pet parents care about. Across the three, our work focuses on companion animals specifically, rather than extrapolation from other species like humans or production animals. To our knowledge, no other oral health postbiotic in the companion animal space has demonstrated clinical fresh-breath and oral-microbiome benefits at this level of validation. See the peer-reviewed research for yourself Animals - human perception of bad breath, VSC reduction Journal of Veterinary Dentistry - oral microbiome Journal of Veterinary Dentistry - human perception of bad breath, VSC reduction ‍ This article is for informational and educational purposes only and is not intended as veterinary or medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Superculture® Pet Oral is an ingredient for use in pet food and supplement products and is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease.

title: Manage ezCater Orders Across Every Restaurant Location
summary: Compare catering performance across locations, find accuracy and timing issues, and manage ezCater alongside your restaurant’s delivery channels.
body_text: Managing ezCater Catering Orders Alongside Delivery Apps If your team runs DoorDash, Uber Eats, and Grubhub like clockwork, ezCater can still catch you off guard. Catering orders don't behave like delivery orders - they're bigger, they're booked further out, and when something goes wrong, it's not one customer who notices, it's an entire office. For multi-location brands adding catering as a growth channel, that difference matters more than it looks like on paper. What Makes Catering Orders Different From Standard Delivery Orders? A catering order through ezCater is a single, larger transaction built around a headcount, a delivery window, and a business customer who's ordering for other people, not just themselves. Standard delivery orders are single-serving, ordered on impulse, and forgiving of small hiccups. Catering orders are booked 24-48 hours ahead, priced per person, and judged by whether the food actually matches what was promised - because the person ordering usually isn't the person eating. That means the operational bar is different. A missing item on a $30 delivery order is annoying. A missing item on a $600 catering order for a 40-person meeting is a problem your customer has to explain to their own boss. Why ezCater Matters for Multi-Location Restaurant Brands ezCater connects restaurants to a large network of workplace buyers - offices, event planners, and recurring meal programs - who order on a completely different cycle than a typical Friday-night delivery customer. For a multi-unit brand, that's a real incremental revenue channel: larger average tickets, more predictable demand once a company becomes a repeat customer, and exposure to buyers who might never have found you through a regular delivery app search. The catch is that ezCater expects consistency across every location that's listed. One store having an off week on order accuracy doesn't just cost that store - it can affect how the whole brand shows up in ezCater's marketplace ranking. The Real Risk: Catering Mistakes Are Expensive and Public A wrong item on a catering order isn't a one-star review from one person, it's a bad experience witnessed by an entire meeting room. And because catering customers often order on a recurring basis - the same office, the same team lunch, week after week - losing that account doesn't just cost you one order, it costs you the whole recurring relationship. Tracking food delivery KPIs like order accuracy and prep timing matters just as much for catering as it does for standard delivery, arguably more, since the margin for error is smaller and the audience per order is bigger. How to Keep ezCater Standards High Across Every Location ezCater's own guidance for restaurants centers on a small number of consistency markers - the same ones that separate a reliable catering partner from one that gets buried in search results. Here's what to keep in view across every location running catering: Confirm headcount math before prep - a serving-size mismatch is the single most common catering complaint. Treat the 24-48 hour lead time as a checkpoint, not a buffer - confirm the order the day before, not the morning of. Use a kitchen checklist at hand-off, not memory - catering orders have more components than a standard bag. Track order accuracy and on-time delivery by location, not just brand-wide - one store's problem can drag down how the whole brand ranks. Keep dietary and packaging details current on your listing - vague menus convert worse and cause more mid-order questions. Route catering complaints and disputes the same way you'd route a delivery order error - quickly, and with evidence. Running Catering and Delivery Through One Operational View The operational trap for multi-location brands is treating catering as a side process - a separate tablet, a separate person checking it, a separate mental model. That's exactly how a catering order gets missed during a lunch rush. The stores that handle catering well are usually the ones that fold it into the same daily rhythm as their DoorDash, Uber Eats, and Grubhub orders: same accuracy standard, same dispute process when a charge looks wrong, same review and reputation tracking when a workplace customer leaves feedback. Talk to a Voosh expert to see how catering fits into a unified delivery operations view. Getting Started With Catering as a Growth Channel If you're already running Voosh across DoorDash, Uber Eats, and Grubhub, adding ezCater to that same operational rhythm is a smaller lift than treating it as a brand-new channel. Start with the stores that already have strong delivery accuracy scores - they're the ones most likely to earn ezCater's reliability standard quickly, and the ones where a first catering push is least likely to go sideways.

title: Transfer on Death Deed in California: July 2026 Guide
summary: Learn how a California transfer on death deed works in July 2026, who qualifies, recording requirements, and how beneficiaries claim property
body_text: A California transfer on death deed lets a property owner pass real estate directly to a named beneficiary at death, with no probate required. It costs far less upfront than a living trust, and the form is widely available. However, the deed only works for certain property types, comes with a creditor liability window, and has certain tax implications. In this article, we'll cover how a California TOD deed works, which property types qualify, recording requirements, how beneficiaries claim property after the owner dies, and how a TOD deed compares to a living trust. Key Takeaways: A California TOD deed transfers property directly to named beneficiaries at death, with no court involvement required. The deed must be signed, notarized, and recorded with the county recorder within 60 days of notarization to be legally valid. Beneficiaries face a 120-day waiting period and a 3-year title insurance delay before they can sell or refinance the property. Only specific property types qualify, including residential property with one to four units, condominium units, and single-family residences on agricultural land of 40 acres or less. The deed is only available to owners who hold title as a sole owner or tenant in common; joint tenancy and community property with right of survivorship already pass outside probate. What Is a Transfer on Death Deed in California? A transfer on death deed in California is a legal document that lets a property owner name one or more beneficiaries to receive real estate automatically at death, without going through probate. The property stays fully under the owner's control during their lifetime. They can sell it, refinance it, or revoke the deed at any time. California's version is called the revocable transfer on death deed, sometimes written as the TOD deed or TODD. It was made permanent under California Probate Code sections 5610 through 5696 after a pilot program that began in 2016. The deed must be signed, notarized, and recorded with the county recorder's office before the owner dies. Recording is what activates the beneficiary designation. A deed that is signed but never recorded has no legal effect. Who Can Use a TOD Deed in California Not every property qualifies. The law limits TOD deeds to specific property types: Residential property with one to four units, where the owner occupies or intends to occupy at least one unit A condominium unit A single-family residence on agricultural land of 40 acres or less The owner must hold title as a sole owner or as a tenant in common . Property held in joint tenancy or community property with right of survivorship already passes outside probate through survivorship, so a TOD deed is generally not needed for those arrangements. {{blog-cta-legal}} What Property Qualifies for a California TOD Deed Not all real property in California qualifies for transfer by TOD deed. The California Probate Code limits eligible property to real property located within the state, which covers most residential homes, condominiums, and vacant land. Commercial real estate and rental properties can also qualify, provided they meet the ownership structure requirements. The key restriction involves how title is held. A TOD deed works only when the transferor holds title as a sole owner or as a tenant in common. Property held in joint tenancy or community property with right of survivorship already passes automatically to the surviving co-owner, making a TOD deed unnecessary and, in practice, ineffective for those ownership types. There are a few additional property types that fall outside the scope of what a TOD deed can transfer: Property already held in a living trust cannot be transferred by TOD deed, since the trust itself governs how that property passes. Real property owned by a business entity, such as an LLC or corporation, is not eligible because the individual does not hold title directly. Property located outside California requires the laws of that state, which may or may not recognize TOD deeds. How to Create a Valid California TOD Deed California law sets out specific requirements a TOD deed must meet to be legally valid. Getting any of these wrong can render the deed ineffective, leaving the property subject to probate. The deed must be in writing and signed by the property owner in front of a notary public. It must clearly identify the property using its legal description, name at least one beneficiary, and include the statutory language indicating the transfer takes effect at death. Once signed and notarized, the deed must be recorded with the county recorder's office in the county where the property is located within 60 days of notarization. Here are the steps in sequence: Complete the deed form using the statutory template, which includes the required declaration language. Forms are available through county recorder offices in Los Angeles, Alameda, San Diego, and other counties, or through the California Courts self-help website. Sign the deed before a notary public. The notarization must occur before recording, and the 60-day recording window begins on the date of notarization, not the date the deed is drafted. File the deed with the county recorder's office in the county where the property sits. Recording fees vary by county but generally fall in the range of $15 to $24 for the first page, with additional per-page fees after that. Complete a Preliminary Change of Ownership Report (PCOR) and submit it alongside the deed at recording. Most county recorder offices require this form at the time of filing. The deed does not need to be delivered to the beneficiary, and the beneficiary does not need to sign or even know about the deed for it to be valid. The property owner retains full ownership and control during their lifetime. {{blog-cta-legal}} How a Beneficiary Claims Property After the Owner Dies After the owner dies, the beneficiary named in a California transfer on death deed can claim the property by filing a few key documents with the county recorder's office where the property is located. The process generally follows these steps: The beneficiary obtains a certified copy of the owner's death certificate, which serves as the official record that the transfer condition has been met. The beneficiary completes and signs an affidavit of survivorship (sometimes called an affidavit of death of transferor), confirming that the named beneficiary is alive and accepting the property. Both the death certificate and the signed affidavit are recorded with the county recorder's office. Once recorded, title passes to the beneficiary without any court involvement, and the beneficiary can take possession, sell, or refinance the property as the new owner. The recording is typically completed within days of submitting the documents, though timelines can vary by county. Los Angeles County, San Diego County, and Alameda County each have their own recorder's office procedures, and fees for recording generally fall in the range of $15 to $25 per page. One important note: if the deceased owner had outstanding debts, creditors may still have claims against the property even after the transfer completes. California law gives creditors a window to file claims following a death, and a beneficiary who receives property through a TOD deed can remain responsible for those obligations up to the value of the property received. How Elayne Supports Families After a TOD Deed Takes Effect A transfer on death deed moves property directly to beneficiaries, but families must still manage a range of administrative steps once it takes effect. After a TOD deed activates, beneficiaries typically need to notify financial institutions, locate and transfer other accounts and assets that fall outside the deed, and coordinate any remaining estate matters. Elayne support families by handling that search and coordination process. For more information, learn about our work and services here . FAQ What is a transfer on death deed in California and how does it work? A California transfer on death deed (also called a revocable TOD deed or TODD) is a legal document that lets a property owner name one or more beneficiaries to receive real estate automatically at death, without probate court involvement. The owner keeps full control of the property during their lifetime and can revoke or update the deed at any time. The deed takes effect only after it is signed, notarized, and recorded with the county recorder's office where the property is located. What are the most common problems with transfer on death deeds in California? The three problems families encounter most often are the three-year title insurance delay (beneficiaries generally cannot sell or refinance until that window closes under Probate Code Section 5696), personal creditor liability up to the value of the property received, and deed failure when the named beneficiary dies before the owner and no alternate is on record. How do I get the Los Angeles County transfer on death deed form? The Los Angeles County transfer on death deed form is available through the LA County Recorder's official website or in person at their offices. San Diego County, Alameda County, and most other California counties provide the same revocable transfer on death deed form through their respective recorder's office websites or self-help counters. The California Courts self-help website also offers a version of the form with basic filing instructions. Once you have the form, it must be signed before a notary public and recorded within 60 days of notarization to be legally valid. Does a TOD deed avoid probate in California? Yes. When the property owner dies, the named beneficiary can claim the property directly by recording an affidavit and a certified death certificate with the county recorder. No court involvement is required. Can a TOD deed be revoked? A California TOD deed is fully revocable at any time before death. The owner can record a revocation form or a new TOD deed to replace or cancel the prior one. Does the beneficiary have to accept the property? No. A beneficiary can disclaim the property within nine months of the owner's death. If they disclaim, the property passes as if they had predeceased the owner. What happens if the beneficiary dies before the owner? If no alternate beneficiary is named and the primary beneficiary dies first, the TOD deed fails and the property goes through probate. Are there income or estate tax consequences? The property receives a stepped-up cost basis at the owner's death, which may reduce real estate inheritance tax liability if the beneficiary later sells. California has no state estate tax, though federal estate tax rules may apply depending on the estate's size. Does a TOD deed protect against the owner's creditors? No. Creditors of the deceased owner can still make claims against the property after death. A TOD deed does not shield the property from outstanding debts or Medi-Cal recovery claims. *Disclaimer: This article is for informational purposes only and does not provide legal, medical, financial, or tax advice.
